title: Christmas Eve

segments.voice: Yesterday, antiphon, the old names for Christ sung one a night, each ending with come. Your line was o come, emmanuel. Which name stayed with you? Day one thousand ten.

The church lights go down until the building is almost dark. Up front, someone lights a single taper and turns to the person beside them, who tips an unlit candle into the flame. That person turns to the next. The light walks down the rows, hand to hand, until the whole room is glowing from below, faces lit like they're around a campfire. And somewhere in the middle of it, everyone starts to sing, softly, a carol the room seems to know by heart. It's late. Some of the children are asleep on their parents' shoulders. Today, Christmas Eve.

Why at night? Because the story starts at night. Luke's Gospel doesn't put the first announcement of the birth in a palace or a temple. It puts it in a field in the dark. In the King James Bible: "And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night." Ordinary night-shift workers, awake while everyone else sleeps. An angel appears, the dark lights up, and they are terrified. Then a multitude of angels praises God, saying: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." So churches gather late, some at midnight, some earlier for families with small children, to be awake when the shepherds were awake. Catholic churches celebrate a Mass at night. Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and others hold candlelight services, and Orthodox churches keep a vigil in their own way, some of them in January, by the older calendar. And the carol in the candlelight? Tradition tells it like this. A priest in a small Austrian village wrote some verses in German, Stille Nacht, and asked a local musician to set them to music for the Christmas Eve service. They sang it with a guitar. Some tellings add that the church organ was broken that night, but that detail may have been added later. However it began, the song traveled, and its English words have become a Christmas Eve fixture: silent night, holy night. It's an odd thing to call that night silent. In Luke, it's full of angels praising God. But the song isn't describing the noise. It's describing the stillness of a sleeping child, and of a world that, for a moment, holds its breath.

Here's the practice: sing a carol. Any carol you know, even just the first verse, even under your breath. Silent Night works, or one from your own childhood. If singing feels like too much, hum it, or say the words slowly. Let the tune carry you back to wherever you first learned it. Then let it go quiet and sit in the stillness after it. If you pray, you can let the angels' line be your prayer: glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace. If you don't, just rest in the quiet the song leaves. The bell holds the time.
Christmas Eve. The night before Christmas, kept with late services and carols by candlelight, because Luke's story begins with shepherds awake in the dark.
Your line: silent night, holy night. Tonight, before you sleep, turn off one more light than usual and give the dark a minute of stillness. Day one thousand ten.

howItsDone: Churches hold services late on Christmas Eve, some at midnight, often with carols and candles passed from person to person; Catholics celebrate Mass during the night, and Orthodox churches keep a vigil, some of them in January by the older Julian calendar.

fork.setup: you're a shepherd on the night shift. a light fills the field and an angel stands in front of you. what does Luke say you feel first?
fork.reveal: the shepherds are terrified first. the angels' praise comes after, and the good news is given to frightened night workers.

notes: Claims rule: no year, names or ages for the carol's origin (Joseph Mohr, Franz Gruber, Oberndorf, 1818 are left out); told as 'tradition tells it'.
The broken-organ detail is flagged as possibly later; confirm.
'Silent night, holy night' appears as the carry and in the voice without quotation marks; the English text is public domain but not on the validator's translation list.
Denominational practices (Catholic Mass during the night, candlelight services, Orthodox vigil on their own calendar) are described generally; confirm.
Editor: Luke 2:13 says the heavenly host was 'praising God, and saying', not singing; voice and fork reveal changed to 'praising'. Dropped 'young' for the carol's priest (age not in a cited text).
Editor 2: review line no longer calls the O Antiphon titles 'the prophets' names', since not all come from the prophets (matches the day 1009 fix).

Audit: 'Orthodox churches keep a vigil ... on their own calendar' implied every Orthodox church differs; many (e.g. Greek, Antiochian) keep 25 December. Voice and howItsDone now say some keep it in January by the older calendar.
